entries.title: Jordan Hicks raising his game in White Sox bullpen
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> reliever Jordan Hicks is getting big results from a small tweak to his delivery that he made while recovering from the lat strain that kept him out of action for a month.</p><p>The hard-throwing right-hander raised his arm slot after “looking at some old video to try to replicate what worked in the past,” the veteran said, helping him find another tick on the 100 mph-plus fastball that put him on the map.</p><p>Hicks struck out two Rangers in his first outing since the All-Star break Monday, extending a 10-game scoreless streak since returning from the injured list June 21. Batters were 3-for-32 against him with 17 strikeouts over that stretch, lowering Hicks’ ERA nearly two full runs down to 3.62.</p><p>If his arm-slot fix sounds simple, Hicks credits another back-to-the-basics routine, too.</p><p>“I’ve also been playing catch more with my four-seam,” Hicks said. “That's what I was doing in ‘23,” when he struck out 81 hitters over 65⅔ innings with the Cardinals and Blue Jays. “With the four-seam, I always want to get a little more ride. That's why I like playing catch with it.”</p><h3><b>Colson nurses calf during laugher</b></h3><p>Colson Montgomery was out of the starting lineup Tuesday as the Sox laid a three-hit egg against Kumar Rocker and the Rangers. Noah Schultz served up five runs and couldn’t escape the fourth inning of a 10-0 loss — but infielder Luisangel Acuna pitched a perfect eighth frame of mop-up duty with a 38 mph curveball.</p><p>Montgomery sat after fouling a ball off his calf and exiting the series opener, but he’s “not worried about it being a long-term thing.”</p><p>“It was a direct hit on my calf muscle,” Montgomery said. “Completely missed my shin guard.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/20/colson-montgomery-all-star-snub-motivation" target="_blank" ><u>his slugging shortstop</u></a> was available off the bench and likely to start Wednesday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> boating Mississippi River near his hometown of downstate Alton over the All-Star break, feasting on fish instead of hitters for one relaxing afternoon.</p><p>Not that it was all good eating. He and some friends were trolling for catfish but spent more time dodging Asian carp leaping out of water.</p><p>“They were literally jumping into the boat,” Hudson said of the invasive species. “Slimy, nasty guys.”</p><p>Hudson, who’s gone from floating around the waiver wire to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/14/alton-illinois-cubs-draft-pick-bryan-hudson-white-sox-cardinals-brewers" >anchoring the back of the Sox’ pen</a>, leapt out of the break with his latest nasty appearance in Toronto. He threw a flawless inning and a third in Sunday’s shutout win to lower his ERA on the season to 2.13 over 43 games.</p><p>“Chucking a few poles in the water is always nice,” the 6-8 reliever said, but he was itching to get back.</p><p>“In the break, it's always that's always on the back of your mind the whole time you're relaxing and whatnot — like, alright, still keep my body in shape, and mentally stay in shape as well to go out there and do it again in a few days,” Hudson said. “So to get that first one out of the way after the break is a good feeling.”</p><h3><b>Naperville Central star signs</b></h3><p>The Sox signed Naperville Central alumnus Colin Barczi as an undrafted free-agent catcher. href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/12/chicago-white-sox-mlb-draft-landon-thome-jim-thome-roch-cholowsky-andrew-benintendi-caleb-bonemer" >Landon Thome</a>, the Hall of Famer Jim’s son from Nazareth Academy, and Brother Rice grad Luke Lawrence, another infielder who went undrafted out of Kentucky.</p><p>Team scouts had projected Barczi as a third- to fifth-round pick out of entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong wowing Cubs brass, who see walk as good as extra-base hit for speedy center fielder
entries.summary: <p>You might have heard that a walk can be as good as a hit.</p><p>But a walk being as good as a double?</p><p>Just another incredible baseball feat courtesy of <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>.</p><p>“The ability to impact on the bases, you can’t pitch around him because it’s an extra-base hit. And if you pitch to him, it might be an extra-base hit,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> said last week. “That’s the real beauty, he can get into scoring position so easily, and you can’t walk guys like that.”</p><p>For Crow-Armstrong, who’s wowing with his improved plate discipline, a walk can be as good as a double, as he can use his speed to easily swipe second base.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong — who started the day fifth in baseball with 25 stolen bases — flashed his speed in Tuesday’s 11-2 win over the Tigers, tripling in his first at-bat. That’s the kind of thing he did with regularity during his breakout 2025 campaign, establishing himself as a human highlight reel.</p><p>But in the same inning — the Cubs sent a dozen men to the plate in a six-run first — he showed what’s made him so newly dangerous this season, drawing a bases-loaded walk that forced in a run; he accounted for three of the team’s 11 walks on the night.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">PCA led off the first inning with a triple and now works a bases-loaded walk... it's still the first inning <a href="https://t.co/Bbt7YjJuui">pic.twitter.com/Bbt7YjJuui</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2079726491995103411?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That’s the evolved PCA that shows the Cubs were onto something when they bet big with a $115 million contract extension.</p><p>“The way he’s played for the last six weeks or so is what you hoped he would get to eventually. He got there really quickly,” Hoyer said. “Obviously, he’s going to have to maintain it and stay there. But some of the great at-bats he’s had?</p><p>“He was facing [lefty reliever <b>Sam] Moll</b> with Cincinnati, and I found myself thinking, ‘Oh, he’s going to walk him.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that is a 180.’ I never would have thought that last year, that he was going to face that kind of guy … and he’s not going to chase a breaking ball away, he’s going to have a disciplined approach. He’s kind of impossible [to pitch to] when you get to that place.</p><p>“This current approach is exactly what we always hoped he could get to. It just came a lot faster than we thought.”</p><p>He’s doing incredible things with his glove, too, turning in another highlight-reel grab Tuesday.</p><p>“They’re plays that nobody else is going to make,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “You’re going to have to watch baseball a long time to find somebody who’s going to make the plays. That’s how good it is.”</p><h3><b>Shaw still waiting to swing</b></h3><p>The Cubs are still waiting for utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> to be entirely free of the symptoms caused by the sprained hand that’s had him sidelined since late last month.</p><p>Counsell touted improvement for Shaw on Tuesday, but despite new imaging showing “significant healing,” Shaw is still waiting to start swinging a bat.</p><p>“We’ve just got to get over that last step. It’s been a stubborn sprain, so to speak. But he’s improving,” Counsell said. “When you swing a baseball bat for a living, it involves the wrist heavily, and we’re just not quite past it.”</p><p>Shaw will head to Arizona to continue working when the Cubs next hit the road.</p><h3><b>Party like it’s 1999</b></h3><p>With his two-run blast Tuesday, <b>Michael Conforto</b> became the second Cub since at least 1901 to hit four pinch-hit homers in a season, matching <b>Glenallen Hill</b>’s franchise record from 1999.</p><p>It was the latest contribution from Conforto, who has carved out a nice role as a part-timer, owning an .824 OPS that’s his best since 2020.</p><p>“It’s always, ‘Can you find a player that can do this job and be successful at it?’” Counsell said. “Michael has done a fabulous job at it, and you feel like it’s a real weapon to have somebody like that.”</p><h3><b>Climbing the list</b></h3><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>’s home run Monday was the 191st of his career and sent him into sole possession of 11th place on the Cubs’ all-time home-run list, passing Hall of Fame outfielder <b>Hack Wilson</b>.</p><p>He’s seven away from tying MVP outfielder <b>Hank Sauer</b>, who’s currently 10th with 198 home runs as a Cub.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true"
